extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, agency rule commenters, and public-interest advocates
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and evaluating public comments to administrative agencies under Stewart's "interest representation model," emphasizing representation of diffuse/public interests, preserving issues for judicial review, and countering agency capture. Useful for advocates aiming to influence rulemaking and create a record for review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest representation model
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern administrative law is animated by an 'interest representation model' that centers participation and representation of affected interests in agency decisionmaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stewart presents this as the central framework for evaluating participation rights and comments: agencies should ensure that all affected interests — not just regulated industries — are represented. Use this model as the overarching lens when assessing the value and aims of a comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Standing expansion — broadening who may seek judicial review of agency action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that broader standing doctrines create opportunities for nontraditional actors to litigate agency decisions. Comments should be drafted with an awareness that their preservation in the record can support standing-based review later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion of participation rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Expansion of participation rights before agencies during rule development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates should take advantage of procedural opportunities (comment periods, hearings, data requests) created by expanded participation rights to introduce perspectives and information agencies might otherwise ignore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate consideration requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequate consideration requirement — agencies must address claims raised by participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments should be crafted to trigger the legal obligation that agencies adequately consider and respond to arguments and evidence in the administrative record; doing so can generate a judicially reviewable failure-to-consider claim if ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the affected interest represented
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifies the affected interest the commenter represents and explains why that interest has been historically under-represented or might be ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly describe who you represent (consumers, environment, communities, beneficiaries) and provide factual or structural reasons showing why the agency is likely to discount or overlook that perspective. This helps establish the comment's representational value under the interest representation model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate non-duplication of industry submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrates the comment is not duplicative of regulated industry submissions — diffuse, consumer, environmental, or beneficiary interests deserve special weight because they have structural barriers to participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how your submission brings distinct viewpoints, data, or analyses that regulated industry actors are unlikely to present. Highlight the unique contributions and the representational gap your comment fills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame arguments to trigger 'adequate consideration' obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Frames arguments to trigger the 'adequately consider' judicial requirement — comments should raise issues the agency must address in the final rule's preamble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure comments so the issues are clear, record-based, and tied to statutory purposes or rulemaking topics; make it straightforward for a court to see that the agency could not plausibly have 'considered' the issue without addressing it in the administrative record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce factual claims and alternative analyses to counter agency capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Counters the risk of agency capture by introducing factual claims, alternative cost estimates, or distributional analyses the regulated industry will not supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete data, alternative methodologies, or distributional impacts to fill informational gaps and challenge industry-dominated narratives. Such submissions can blunt capture and force agencies to confront contested empirical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assert procedural rights where the record is incomplete
rubrics_metrics.description: Asserts a procedural right (e.g., to additional data disclosure, supplemental comment period, hearing) where the record is incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When essential information is missing, explicitly request further procedures (data disclosure, extended comment, hearing) and explain why the existing record is inadequate for reasoned decisionmaking. This both improves the record and creates procedural bases for challenge if ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface interests the agency would otherwise discount
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment surface an interest the agency would otherwise discount?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the submission brings forward perspectives or stakes (e.g., diffuse consumers, low-income communities) that are not salient to the agency or regulated industry, thereby justifying special consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force the agency to confront otherwise-avoided tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment force the agency to confront a tradeoff it would prefer to elide?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good comments identify concrete policy tradeoffs (cost vs. benefit, distributional effects, statutory aims) and frame them so the agency must acknowledge and justify its chosen balance in the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlarge the universe of facts and values the agency must address
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment enlarge the universe of facts/values the agency must address on the record?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide new evidence, framing, or normative considerations that meaningfully broaden what the agency must consider — beyond narrow technical points to include social, distributional, or statutory-purpose-related facts and values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve objections to lay foundation for judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment lay a foundation for judicial review by preserving an objection?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure objections are clearly presented and tied to the administrative record and statutory standards so they are preserved for possible later litigation under adequacy or procedural-review doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mere preference-assertion; supply reasoned statutory justifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation without substantive constraints can produce interest-group pluralism; effective comments should not merely assert preferences but should provide reasoned justifications grounded in the statute's purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor arguments in statutory text, legislative purpose, or record evidence. Avoid simple advocacy slogans or unsupported assertions; courts and agencies give weight to reasoned, law-and-evidence-based submissions.
